title: Talking to Leaders When They Fall Out of Favor
author: Admired Leadership
summary: An argument about relationship-building disguised as an observation about disgrace. The author begins with the unremarkable fact that capable people are fired, demoted, passed over and publicly diminished, then turns to what happens next: the people around them quietly withdraw, either from fear of contamination or from a calculation that a leader who can no longer confer advantage is no longer worth knowing. That withdrawal is read as diagnostic — it exposes how thin and transactional the fallen leader's network always was. The counterintuitive move follows: the vacuum created by everyone else's retreat is precisely the opening for anyone who genuinely admires the person, because a leader stripped of influence can only interpret a new approach as sincere. Connections formed in that window tend to become durable friendships that could not have been built while the leader still held power. The piece closes on the pragmatic coda that talented people usually recover, and when they do they remember who stayed.
points: Withdrawal after a fall is framed as evidence about the relationships themselves — utilitarian ties dissolve the moment the utility does.

The author's central mechanism: because the fallen leader has no favours left to grant, they can only read a new overture as grounded in affinity rather than advantage, which is why the trust forms so fast.
The window is described as temporary — for genuinely talented people the fall is a chasm in the road rather than an ending, and the access it opens closes again on recovery.
The prescription is unglamorous and specific: the only thing required to build the connection is a request to engage.
Not following the crowd toward people in favour is presented as a defining behaviour of those who are actually good at relationships, not merely a kindness.
quotes: On occasion, even good people get fired, fall from grace, get demoted, fail to secure the top job, and lose their reputation.
The fear of getting stained by whatever misfortune occurred is always on the minds of those who are most about themselves.
This fair-weathered attitude isolates leaders and illustrates how thin and utilitarian many of their relationships really were.
Because the leader can no longer influence, they rightly presume this new relationship is grounded in affinity, learning, and mutual insight.
Relationships that arise during such moments of personal crisis often become rich, meaningful, and lifelong friendships that benefit both parties.
When they recover their mojo, they turn to authentic relationships with those who didn’t abandon them when it mattered most.
